y1: The Pharisees' hand washing was not about hygiene, but a religious purification ritual. It was the tradition of the elders that extended a rule meant only for priests in the Law to everyone.
y2: Jesus asks a counter-question: isn't the tradition of swearing “Corban” (dedicated to God) to avoid honoring parents canceling God's commandment? Then He quotes Isaiah 29:13: “These people honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.”
y3: Tradition itself can be good. The problem arises when human tradition is placed above God's commandment. Church culture must face the same question: does this tradition bring me closer to God, or does it hide God?
y5: “Not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man; but that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man.” Jesus moves the place of purity from the hands to the heart.
y6: “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.” The problem is not in the outside world, but inside me.
y7: Jesus calls the Pharisees “blind leading the blind.” A person who cannot see their own heart cannot guide others on the right path. This connects to the story of the “plank” in 7:3–5.
y8: The faith on the farthest edge
y9: Jesus went to the Gentile region of Tyre and Sidon. The woman was a Gentile, a woman, and the mother of a demon-possessed daughter. Moreover, “Canaan” was an ancient enemy of Israel in the Old Testament. Such a woman called Jesus “Son of David.”
y10: Despite Jesus' silence and words that sounded like a rejection, the woman did not back down. “Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.” Jesus is amazed: “Woman, great is your faith.” This contrasts with the “you of little faith” spoken to Peter in 14:31.
y11: The sequence of Jesus' mission (Israel first, 10:6) is visible, but the conversation itself becomes a stage to reveal the woman's faith. The woman claims no rights, relying only on grace. It is a faith that says even a “crumb” is enough. Because Jesus' grace is so great that even a crumb will overflow.
y12: A feast in the land of the Gentiles
y13: East of Galilee (likely in the Decapolis, a Gentile region), Jesus healed many sick people, and the people “glorified the God of Israel.” Gentiles are praising the God of Israel.
y14: Then He feeds four thousand people. While the five thousand in chapter 14 were in Jewish territory, this time it is in Gentile territory. The “crumb” mentioned by the Canaanite woman has now become an overflowing feast for the Gentiles.
y15: After the five thousand, twelve baskets were left over (the twelve tribes of Israel), and after the four thousand, seven baskets were left over. 7 is a number of perfection, or it symbolizes all nations, recalling the seven nations of Canaan (Deut. 7:1).
verse: “She said, ‘Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters' table.’ Then Jesus answered her, ‘Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour.”
prayer: Jesus, thank You for looking at the heart, not the outside. Let me love God with my heart, not just my lips. Erase the boundaries I have drawn, and give me great faith to ask to the end, relying on grace rather than rights, like the Canaanite woman. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: tradition of the elders. These are the rules passed down by the rabbis to explain and supplement the Law of Moses. They were later written down as the Mishnah. It started with a good intention to protect the Law like a “fence.”
d1: heart. In the Bible, the heart is not only about emotions, but the center that thinks and makes decisions. “Blessed are the pure in heart” (5:8).
d2: Canaan. Mark calls her a “Syrophoenician woman,” but Matthew intentionally uses the Old Testament name “Canaan.” It emphasizes that the one farthest away came the closest. The Canaanite woman Rahab is also in Jesus' genealogy (1:5).
d3: crumb. A tiny piece that falls from the table. The woman believed that even with this, her daughter could be healed. “Dog” (kynarion) refers to a small puppy kept in the house.
